As \(x\to2^+\), the denominator \(x-2\) is positive and tends to \(0\), so
\[
\frac{1}{x-2}\to\infty.
\]
As \(x\to2^-\), the denominator is negative and tends to \(0\), so
\[
\frac{1}{x-2}\to-\infty.
\]

questions.prompt: A function is defined by \(f(x)=x+1\) for \(x<1\), and \(f(x)=3x-1\) for \(x>1\). Does \(\lim_{x\to1}f(x)\) exist?
questions.answer:
The left-hand limit is
\[
\lim_{x\to1^-}(x+1)=2.
\]
The right-hand limit is
\[
\lim_{x\to1^+}(3x-1)=2.
\]
The one-sided limits agree, so the two-sided limit exists and equals \(2\).

Divide numerator and denominator by \(x^3\):
\[
\frac{6-1/x^2}{2+5/x+1/x^3}.
\]
As \(x\to\infty\), the reciprocal terms tend to \(0\), so the limit is
\[
\frac{6}{2}=3.
\]
